https://wtvbam.com/2026/08/07/hungary-ex.text: Sign In Search News Weather Cancellations Events Obituaries Blogs & Podcasts Blogs Podcasts On Air Hungary expects Danube to rise but nuclear plant still facing output curbs By Thomson Reuters Aug 7, 2026 | 8:21 AM BUDAPEST, Aug 7 (Reuters) – The nuclear plant that supplies nearly half of Hungary’s electricity will likely continue running at reduced capacity despite a rise in water levels on the Danube river which helps cool it, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said ​on Friday. The level of the Danube is set to temporarily rise thanks to ‌rains in Austria, but the situation at the Paks nuclear plant remains “difficult”, Magyar said in a Facebook video. The plant has been running at 10% of its capacity since last week due to a prolonged heatwave, as across much of Europe, and record-low water river levels. “We must find a solution for operating the Paks nuclear plant ‌as ​the Hungarian economy cannot work without the plant for months,” ⁠Magyar said later on Friday ⁠at a briefing. GOVERNMENT WORKING ON SOLUTIONS Last week Magyar asked companies and citizens to cut back electricity use in the evening hours and dimmed decorative lighting on Budapest’s historic buildings to save energy. Magyar also said on Friday that temperatures were expected to drop and the ​country’s energy and water supplies were stable, which meant there was no longer need for cutbacks. However, Magyar said the situation at Paks remains “difficult”, and that the government was working on ⁠solutions if low water levels become permanent. “We expect the ⁠water level to rise a good 20 cm in the next few ​days, however, as there is no rain expected again from tomorrow, this rise is expected to ​be temporary,” Magyar said. Later Magyar said there was a “slight chance” that another turbine ‌at the plant can be restarted on Monday, doubling its output. PLANNED EXPANSION TO BE REVIEWED Magyar also said that a review of the plant’s planned expansion has become all the more necessary and that it is already costing double what was projected at the start of planning. Former Prime ⁠Minister Viktor Orban’s government awarded the Paks 2 project in 2014 without a tender to Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom, and it has been delayed by years. Magyar also said that according to current ⁠plans Paks 2 would also ‌be cooled by the Danube. “It is certain that the Paks 2 ⁠project needs to be renegotiated from this perspective as well,” he ​said, while ‌also mentioning other methods including cooling towers. Magyar also said the government ​will examine ⁠what investments were needed to make Hungary’s energy and water supplies more resilient. Magyar said last week that Hungary will develop 4 gigawatts of wind energy capacity by 2030 to diversify its energy sources. On Friday, he said that the government will put out a tender for 700 MW of wind power generation capacity by August 31. http://www.europesun.com/news/279233759/.text: No EU membership for Ukraine unless it confronts Nazi-linked past - Polish parliament speaker RT.com 11 Aug 2026, 09:22 GMT+10 Kiev must stop honoring nationalist forces responsible for massacres of Polish civilians during World War II, Wlodzimierz Czarzasty has said Ukraine must stop honoring Nazi-linked nationalist paramilitaries that massacred Polish civilians during World War II if it wants to join the EU, Polish parliament speaker Wlodzimierz Czarzasty has said. Modern-day Ukraine honors the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and its military wing, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), as part of the country's national liberation movement. The OUN collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, while the UPA was responsible for the deaths of tens of thousands of Poles in 1943-1944 in what is now western Ukraine. Polish estimates put the death toll at up to 100,000, and Warsaw recognizes the massacres as genocide. Ukrainian nationalists also participated in anti-Jewish pogroms during the war. Speaking after talks with Ukrainian parliament speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk on Monday, Czarzasty said he supported Ukraine's bid to join the EU but warned that membership would require Ukrainians to "rethink all aspects of their history." "The EU is, after all, about democracy and values. It's not just an ATM," he said, adding that European integration also means "calling genocide genocide" and acknowledging historical crimes. In Ukraine, streets and buildings are named after WWII-era nationalist leaders, including OUN chief Stepan Bandera and Roman Shukhevich, who served as a deputy commander of the German-led Nachtigall Battalion and later commanded the UPA. Ukrainian military units and officials also frequently use the UPA's red-and-black colors alongside Ukraine's blue-and-yellow national flag. In June, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky added the honorary title "Heroes of the UPA" to the name of an active commando unit, sparking outrage in Poland. Ukrainian authorities have also advanced plans for a national pantheon and, in May, reburied Andrey Melnik, one of the OUN's leaders, with state honors. Polish President Karol Nawrocki responded by stripping Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland's highest state honor, which had been awarded by his predecessor. Multiple Ukrainian officials, in turn, returned their Polish decorations in solidarity with Zelensky, while Polish officials returned Ukrainian awards. The European Parliament backed Poland's position last month, condemning Zelensky's decision to honor the UPA as an "unnecessary and unprovoked escalation" that disregarded Polish grief and was "not in line with European values." Despite the dispute over historical atrocities, Poland remains one of Ukraine's biggest supporters in its conflict with Russia. Moscow has repeatedly condemned the glorification of Nazi collaborators in Ukraine and has stated that one of its goals in the conflict is to "denazify" the country. https://www.c-mw.net/vilnius-picks-winni.text: Vilnius picks winning design for Lithuania's first congress centre Europe | Iain Stirling 27 August 2026, 4:43pm Vilnius has selected a design for what will be Lithuania’s first purpose-built congress centre, giving the city a route into bidding for events it has never been able to host. The winning proposal, “THREE”, is by Lithuanian practice IMPLMNT Architects . The 31,500sqm venue will sit between the Lithuanian Parliament and Geležinio Vilko Street on the Neris river, with a 2,000-seat plenary hall, 17 flexible event spaces and capacity for up to 4,500 delegates across simultaneous events. The open international competition launched in December 2025 with a €100,000 prize fund and drew 28 submissions. Of those, 17 met procurement requirements and went forward to jury evaluation. Second place went to “UNFOLD” by Studija Heima, and third to “FOREST FORUM VILNIUS” by KRS. Mayor of Vilnius Valdas Benkunskas said: “The winning proposal combines architectural quality with long-term value for the city. It will strengthen Vilnius’ international profile, contribute to economic growth, and open a new section of the Neris riverfront for public use.” The competition also asked architects to rework a publicly accessible stretch of the riverfront next to a planned pedestrian bridge. Aurimas Syrusas, architect at IMPLMNT Architects, said: “The design responds carefully to its surroundings – the Parliament, the Neris embankment and the future pedestrian bridge. Its fragmented volumes step down towards both the river and Parliament, ensuring the new complex complements these important landmarks while creating an open and welcoming public space.” The winner was chosen by an international jury that included Danish architect Helle Juul, co-founder of Juul Frost Arkitekter; Vilnius chief city architect Laura Kairienė; and Go Vilnius chief executive Dovilė Aleksandravičienė. Vilnius will now open negotiations with IMPLMNT Architects on the design contract for the venue and its surrounding public spaces. Construction is scheduled for completion by the end of 2031. https://www.politico.eu/article/this-sum.text: BRUSSELS — Extreme heat killed more than 50,000 Europeans this summer. Climate change was responsible for two-thirds of the death toll. Those are the stark findings from two new peer-reviewed studies in the academic journal Nature Health, marking the first comprehensive assessment of fatalities during this year’s record-breaking heat waves. The figures come from around 850 cities across Europe, meaning the full death toll, including rural areas, is higher still. The scientists also found that this summer was the deadliest so far this century, far outstripping previous records. Advertisement Advertisement “I think we can be quite confident in stating that the summer of 2026 is likely to have been the worst on record for heat-related mortality across much of Europe,” said study lead author Clair Barnes, an extreme weather researcher at Imperial College London. “These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health. Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them,” she added. Scientists from Imperial College and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine examined 854 cities in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Norway and Switzerland, home to about 40% of the 30 countries’ population. The first study, published earlier this month , looked at climate-linked mortality between 2000 and 2025, while the second study , released on Friday, focused on 2026. Both papers estimated heat-related excess deaths by analyzing temperature records and historical heat-mortality models, a method the researchers say has consistently produced results mirroring official statistics later released by governments. To isolate the role of climate change, the scientists then compared the actual weather seen in these cities to a temperature model representing a world without global warming. Advertisement Advertisement They found that more than 50,000 heat-related excess deaths occurred in those cities this summer, with around 32,000 attributable to climate change driving up temperatures. The studies also showed how exceptionally deadly this year’s summer proved. Between 2000 and 2025, the first paper found a total of 430,000 heat-related deaths, with around half caused by climate change. The 2026 figures eclipsed the previous records of 29,000 deaths in 2022 and 28,000 in 2003. Almost a third of this summer’s heat-related deaths occurred during Europe’s late June heat wave that smashed several temperature records. And while the elderly were the worst-affected population group, the death toll of this summer included around 6,000 people under the age of 65. “The burden was greater among older adults. People aged 85 and over accounted for roughly half of the estimated deaths,” said Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, study co-author and assistant professor at Imperial College. “However, heat-related mortality was not limited to the older populations,” he added. “Even among younger adults, people aged between 20 and 44, we estimated more than 800 excess deaths.” Advertisement Advertisement
